channel.title: Kentucky History Drive
channel.description: New Kentucky history stories on Kentucky History Drive, newest first.

item.title: Blackfish, Chillicothe war chief
item.description: Blackfish (c. 1729–1779), war chief of the Chillicothe Shawnee, refused to give up Kentucky hunting ground after Dunmore’s War.

item.title: Burlington: from Craig’s Camp to Boone’s seat
item.description: In June 1799 Boone County’s first court fixed the county seat at Craig’s Camp, 74 acres at the headwaters of Allens Fork.

item.title: Campbellsville: from Andrew Campbell’s lots to a county seat
item.description: Andrew Campbell of Augusta County, Virginia, was selling lots and keeping a gristmill and a tavern by 1814, and the legislature established Campbellsville in 1817.

item.title: Capt. Robert Johnson and Big Crossing Station
item.description: Robert Johnson (1745–1815) founded Johnson’s Station in 1783 at the bison ford on Elkhorn Creek in Scott County, the place called Great Crossing.

item.title: Tinsley Hill: Mississippian town under Lake Barkley
item.description: Tinsley Hill (15Ly18), in Lyon County, is a late prehistoric stone-grave cemetery and village on the Cumberland.

item.title: Little Turtle and Kentucky’s 1790 militia disaster
item.description: Little Turtle, Mihšihkinaahkwa in the Miami language, was a Miami war leader who had lived at Turtletown on the Eel River.

item.title: Mann’s Lick, Louisville’s forgotten salt town
item.description: Mann’s Lick was a salt lick just north of the present-day Fairdale neighborhood of Louisville.

item.title: Owingsville: a town named on a wager
item.description: In 1795 Colonel Thomas Dye Owings was sent from Maryland to Kentucky by his father to operate some of the first iron furnaces in the region.

item.title: Red River Gorge: sandstone arches and the dam fight
item.description: The Red River Gorge is a canyon system on the Red River in east-central Kentucky, part of the Pottsville Escarpment, carved over millions of years by erosion and weathering into high sandstone cliffs, rock shelters, waterfalls, and natural bridges.

item.title: Simon Girty, the frontier’s most hated interpreter
item.description: Simon Girty was born in 1741 at Chambers’ Mills in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania.

item.title: Cornstalk (Hokoleskwa), from Point Pleasant to Fort Randolph
item.description: Hokoleskwa, “a blade of corn,” called Cornstalk by the colonists, was a leader of the Mekoche division of the Shawnee and their main war chief in Lord Dunmore’s War.

item.title: Esther Whitley: over the Cumberlands in 1775
item.description: Esther Gill Fullen (1755–1833) was born in Augusta County, Virginia, and married William Whitley there; together they had eight daughters and three sons.

item.title: Liberty Hall: John Brown’s house in the new capital
item.description: In 1786 James Wilkinson bought much of the land that is now downtown Frankfort and laid out the town, naming its streets for friends, famous people and places, and himself.

item.title: Old Mulkey Meetinghouse, 1804
item.description: South of Tompkinsville in Monroe County, off KY 1446, stands a log meetinghouse built in 1804 for the Mill Creek Baptist Church, a congregation of pioneer Baptists from the Carolinas led by John and Philip Mulkey.

item.title: Pine Mountain and Pound Gap
item.description: Pine Mountain is a single ridge of the Appalachians running about 125 miles from near Pioneer, Tennessee, to near Elkhorn City, Kentucky.

item.title: Carlisle: a county seat in Kincart’s peach orchard
item.description: Nicholas County was formed in 1799 from parts of Mason and Bourbon counties and named for Col. George Nicholas, a Revolutionary War veteran who became a popular lawyer in early Kentucky.

item.title: John Bradford and the Kentucke Gazette
item.description: John Bradford (1749–1830), born in Prince William County, Virginia, first came to Kentucky with a surveying party in 1775 and moved his family out in 1784 or 1785.

item.title: Horse series: the Kentucky Association and Lexington’s race course
item.description: On July 23, 1826, Bluegrass horsemen formed the Kentucky Association to promote the breeding and racing of Thoroughbreds.

item.title: Mantle Rock and the Trail of Tears, 1838–39
item.description: On the Northern Route of the Trail of Tears, Cherokee detachments entered Kentucky on the Port Royal Road in Todd County, camped at Hopkinsville and Princeton, followed the Salem–Golconda Road through Salem past Mantle Rock, and crossed the Ohio at Berry's Ferry to Golconda, Illinois, before heading west to the Mississippi.

item.title: Treaty of Logstown, 1752
item.description: Logstown (French Chiningué) stood on the Ohio River near present Ambridge and Baden in Beaver County, Pennsylvania.

item.title: Athiamiowee: the Warriors’ Path through Kentucky
item.description: The Warriors' Path ran from the Ohio River opposite the mouth of the Scioto (Lower Shawneetown, near present South Portsmouth) south past Eskippakithiki in Clark County, across the Red and Kentucky rivers near Irvine, along War Fork and Goose Creek to Flat Lick, over the Cumberland River at Pineville, and through Cumberland Gap toward the Cherokee Overhill towns on the Little Tennessee River.

item.title: Cane Ridge Meeting House and the 1801 camp meeting
item.description: About six miles east of Paris in Bourbon County, Presbyterian settlers built a meeting house of blue ash logs in 1791 on a ridge named for its canebrakes.

item.title: Gen. James Wilkinson, Kentucky’s “Agent 13”
item.description: James Wilkinson (1757–1825), born in Maryland, was brevetted a brigadier general in November 1777, at 20, after carrying news of the Saratoga victory to Congress, though he was soon pushed to resign.

item.title: Hodgenville: from Hodgen’s Mill to a county seat
item.description: The LaRue County seat grew up around a gristmill.

item.title: Old Fort Earthworks: Hopewell’s square on the Ohio
item.description: Across the Ohio River from Portsmouth, Ohio, near South Portsmouth in Greenup County, Middle Woodland builders (about 200 BC to AD 500) raised the westernmost part of the Portsmouth Earthworks.

item.title: Daniel Trabue, the pioneer who wrote it all down
item.description: Daniel Trabue (1760–1840), raised in Chesterfield County, Virginia, and descended from French Huguenots, came through Cumberland Gap as a teenager with his brother James and spent nearly three years in Kentucky, at Fort Boonesborough and Logan’s Fort.

item.title: McLean Drift Bank: Kentucky’s first commercial coal mine (1820)
item.description: Explorer Thomas Walker found coal in what would become Kentucky in 1750 and burned it in his campfire, but nobody mined it for sale for another seventy years.

item.title: Pilot Knob, Boone’s overlook
item.description: Pilot Knob, a 730-foot sandstone outcrop in Powell County, is believed to be where Daniel Boone and John Finley first looked out over the Bluegrass.

item.title: Red Bird River Petroglyphs: the carved rock that fell onto KY 66
item.description: A 50-ton sandstone block cut with petroglyphs sat in a cliff above the Red Bird River near Eriline in Clay County.

item.title: Russellville: from Big Boiling Spring to a county seat
item.description: The Logan County seat started as a spring with a string of names: Big Boiling Spring, Gasper Butcher’s Spring, Butcher’s Station.

item.title: Flemingsburg, Stockton’s town
item.description: Col. John Fleming came into the hill country south of Limestone in 1776 to mark and improve land, served as an officer in the Revolution, and built Fleming's Station in 1788.

item.title: Frederick Stitzel’s barrel racks, 1879
item.description: Before 1879, Kentucky warehousemen rolled barrels into lines on the floor, laid a pair of wooden rails across them, and rolled another row on top, three or four barrels high.

item.title: Gen. Charles Scott and Petersburg
item.description: Revolutionary War general Charles Scott first saw Kentucky in 1785, coming down the Ohio to Limestone, and moved his family out in 1787 to land near present-day Versailles, where he built a two-story log house, a stockade, and a tobacco inspection warehouse at what became Scott's Landing.

item.title: Jeptha Knob, Shelby County’s buried crater
item.description: About eight miles east of Shelbyville near Clay Village, Jeptha Knob rises some 300 feet above the surrounding farmland and is the highest point in the Bluegrass.

item.title: Treaty of Greenville, 1795: the line to the Kentucky River
item.description: On August 3, 1795, at Fort Greenville in western Ohio, leaders of twelve nations (Wyandot, Delaware, Shawnee, Odawa, Ojibwe, Potawatomi, Miami, Eel River, Wea, Kickapoo, Piankashaw, and Kaskaskia) made peace with Gen. Anthony Wayne, a year after their defeat at Fallen Timbers.

item.title: Carrollton from Port William
item.description: Where the Kentucky River empties into the Ohio, Gen. Charles Scott built a blockhouse in 1789 to protect settlers, according to the Kentucky Historical Society marker at Point Park.

item.title: Col. John Hardin of Pleasant Run
item.description: John Hardin was born in Virginia in 1753.

item.title: Hidden River Cave under Horse Cave
item.description: Hidden River Cave lies directly beneath the town of Horse Cave in Hart County, and its main entrance is a large sinkhole at 119 East Main Street.

item.title: Rowlandton Mound Site (15McN3), Paducah
item.description: The Rowlandton Mound Site (15MCN3) is a Mississippian town site inside present-day Paducah, on the edge of an old oxbow lake a little south of the Ohio River.

item.title: Tellico cession, 1805, south of the Cumberland
item.description: On October 25, 1805, at Tellico, U.S. commissioners Return J. Meigs and Daniel Smith concluded a treaty with Cherokee chiefs and headmen—among the signers were Path Killer, Doublehead, Glass and John Jolly—in which the Cherokee gave up all the land they had claimed north of a line that began at the mouth of the Duck River.

item.title: Andalex Village (15Hk22), Hopkins County
item.description: The Andalex site sits on a bluff overlooking the Pond River in Hopkins County, where Mississippian farmers occupied a mound center from AD 1175 to 1275.

item.title: Camp Nelson, Jessamine County
item.description: The U.S. Army established Camp Nelson in central Kentucky in April 1863 as a fortified supply depot, forward base and hospital, part of the Union effort to liberate East Tennessee.

item.title: Louisville and Portland Canal
item.description: The Falls of the Ohio form the only barrier to navigation between Pittsburgh and New Orleans, and cargo was portaged around them except for a few weeks of high water each spring.

item.title: Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill
item.description: In 1805 three Shaker missionaries—John Meacham, Issachar Bates and Benjamin Seth Youngs—left New York and traveled mostly on foot to Kentucky, and in August found three Kentuckians willing to listen, who soon became the state’s first Shaker converts.

item.title: William Hoy and Hoy’s Station
item.description: William Hoy established Hoy’s Station in Madison County in 1781, with help from George Boone, according to a Boone-family genealogy; a Filson Historical Society study of pioneer forts and stations places it about six miles northwest of present-day Richmond.

item.title: Blue Jacket (Weyapiersenwah)
item.description: Shawnee war chief Blue Jacket (c. 1743–1810) first appears in written records at his Scioto town in 1773, fought at Point Pleasant in Lord Dunmore’s War, and allied with the British through the Revolution.

item.title: Louisville & Nashville Railroad opens the interior
item.description: Kentucky chartered the Louisville & Nashville on March 5, 1850, to build south toward Nashville; Tennessee authorized the extension in 1851.

item.title: McAfee Station on the Salt River
item.description: In May 1773, Virginia’s McAfee Company—brothers James, Robert, and George, with James McCoun Jr. and Samuel Adams—surveyed fertile Salt River bottomlands in today’s Mercer County.

item.title: Slone Site (15Pi11), Pike County
item.description: On the north bank of the Levisa Fork of the Big Sandy, Slone was a late Middle Fort Ancient circular village occupied about 1350–1400 CE for roughly thirty to forty-five years.

item.title: Washington, Mason County
item.description: In 1785 Arthur Fox and Baptist preacher William Wood bought about 700 acres and laid out a one-mile-square town; Virginia chartered Washington in 1786—widely cited as the first American settlement named for George Washington while Kentucky was still part of Virginia.

item.title: William Calk’s 1775 journal
item.description: William Calk walked from Prince William County, Virginia, by Rapidan and over the Blue Ridge, down the Valley to Crow's Ferry, Pepper's Ferry on the New River and Fort Chiswell, across the Clinch country to Martin's Station in Powell Valley, through Cumberland Gap on April 8, and along Boone's Trace by the Cumberland, Laurel and Rockcastle rivers to Boonesborough on April 20, 1775.

item.title: Christopher Gist, 1750–51
item.description: Christopher Gist set out from Cresap's Old Town on the Potomac on October 31, 1750, went by Shannopin's Town and Logstown to the Wyandot town on the Muskingum, and on to Lower Shawneetown at the mouth of the Scioto, with a side trip to Pickawillany on the Great Miami. On March 12, 1751 he crossed into Kentucky and went down the south side of the Ohio to a salt lick said to be 15 miles above the Falls, then turned south across the Red River, which he called the little Cuttaway, and struggled east through the mountains to the Bluestone and the New River, reaching his home on the Yadkin on May 18.

item.title: George Rogers Clark
item.description: George Rogers Clark's men left Corn Island at the Falls of the Ohio on June 24, 1778, rowed down the Ohio to the old French Fort Massac, marched about 120 miles overland to take Kaskaskia on the night of July 4, and sent Bowman to take Cahokia, while Father Gibault and Leonard Helm won over Vincennes. In February 1779 Clark marched about 180 miles from Kaskaskia through flooded country to retake Vincennes, where Hamilton surrendered Fort Sackville on February 25.

item.title: Thomas Walker and Cumberland Gap
item.description: Dr. Thomas Walker left Castle Hill in Albemarle County on March 6, 1750, crossed the Blue Ridge and the New, Holston and Clinch rivers, went through Cave Gap (Cumberland Gap) on April 13, named the Cumberland River, and raised a cabin near present Barbourville. He then looped north on the Warriors' Path toward the Red River, east past Paintsville to the Levisa Fork ("Louisa"), over to the Tug Fork and the New and Greenbrier rivers, and home by Hot Springs and Staunton on July 13.
